title: Design by Contract
story: Bertrand Meyer, the inventor of Design by Contract, tells a story: a team spent months debugging a payment system. When they finally wrote contracts FIRST, they found 23 edge cases in the first hour — edge cases no one had considered because they started with implementation.
why: Writing contracts before the function body surface-tests your design against reality — if you can't write the contract, you don't understand the problem.
analogy: Writing the contract first is like writing the test before the code — it proves you know what 'correct' means before you start building.
try_it: Design a `transfer_funds` function between two Inventory items. Follow the three steps: write signature, write contract, write body. What preconditions must hold? What postconditions must be guaranteed? Think about edge cases (same item, zero transfer).
tips: If you can't write the `requires` clause, you haven't thought about what the function NEEDS from the caller
If you can't write the `ensures` clause, you haven't defined what 'done' means for this function
A contract that's hard to write is a design smell — simplify the function's responsibility
common_mistakes: Skipping the contract step because 'it's obvious what this function does' — obvious to YOU isn't obvious to the next developer
Writing contracts that are too weak ('ensures: true') — every function should guarantee SOMETHING
Writing contracts that are too strong — 'ensures: account.balance == 100.0' is wrong if it depends on input
